artboards.title: B — the badge at the top

annotations.text:
THE NOTE THIS ANSWERS

“Even when toggled on, it doesn’t indicate that this is about making the house’s devices available as Matter devices, to be shared with other Matter-compatible ecosystems. It’s a good selling point — why should we be shy about showcasing it?”

The screen that exists says Share, and says the house keeps working with the apps removed. Both true, and both written as if the feature were a risk to be reassured about. The word Matter never appears. Nothing says the lights BECOME something over there. A household that already owns a HomePod cannot tell from this page that it has just become useful.

All three boards below say the same true thing. They differ only in how much of the page they spend saying it.

A — A PAGE OF ROWS

The page as it is, with the words fixed and nothing else. A lede that names Matter and says what happens; then the four rows.

FOR: it is the same page as every other settings page, which is the whole argument of docs/settings.md — four nouns, no page of knobs. It reads quickly and it will never look dated.

AGAINST: it showcases nothing. The lede is a paragraph, and paragraphs are the thing people skip. On a wall at head height this is a page somebody reads once and never again, which is fine for Backup and wrong for the one feature worth showing a visitor.

B — THE BADGE AT THE TOP

A hero: WORKS WITH MATTER, one large line, and four named cards — Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa, and SmartThings carrying “…and anything else that speaks Matter”. The rows follow underneath, unchanged.

FOR: it answers the question a person actually has — does this work with the thing I own — in one glance, by name. It is the shape every product on a shelf uses, because it works. And it stays true when the door is shut: the cards are what it works WITH, not what holds it, so they never go stale.

AGAINST: it is the loudest thing in a panel that is quiet everywhere else, and the four cards are furniture that never changes. There is a risk it reads as an advertisement on somebody’s own wall, which is the one place an advertisement is unwelcome.

C — THE MECHANISM, DRAWN

A diagram: three of the house’s own things on the left, one Matter mark in the middle, the three apps on the right.

FOR: it is the only one that explains what the feature IS rather than what it works with. “Your things become Matter devices” is an abstraction until you see a kettle on one side and Apple Home on the other. It also quietly sets the expectation that the hub is in the middle — which is what makes the rest of the page (what is shared, and the lock switch) make sense.

AGAINST: a diagram earns its place once and then costs its space forever. Somebody who has understood it on Tuesday still scrolls past it on Friday, and the rows — which are the part you come back for — start halfway down the page.

WHAT IS COMMON TO ALL THREE

The word Matter, said plainly and early. The ecosystems named. A count of real things rather than an abstraction — 14 things, not “your devices”. Its own door in This house, so the feature is discoverable without opening The hub. And the lock switch kept exactly where it is, with the sentence that is the decision.

ONE THING NONE OF THEM DOES, DELIBERATELY: no Matter logo, and nowhere does it say Matter certified. That mark is the CSA’s and using it needs certification this hub does not have — the bridge is on a test vendor id. Naming the standard in text is fine and is what these boards do. docs/matter.md, Certification.

DECIDED, 18 SEPTEMBER 2026 — C, WITH A BADGE OF OUR OWN

C is built. The map is drawn from the house's own things — the brain hands the panel the first three by name, through the same gates the bridge is handed, so what is drawn on its way out is what would actually go out. A re-typed siren is not in the picture for the same reason it is not in the list.

And the badge asked for is drawn rather than borrowed. The Connectivity Standards Alliance's own guidelines say their brands “may only be used on Products … that have been Certified with the Alliance”, and this bridge runs on test vendor id 0xfff1. Wearing their mark now would breach that and would tell a household this hub is certified when it is not — which is the one lie a page about trust cannot afford.

So the badge is a hub with three things on it, in the panel's own gold, with the word Matter under it. It is ours, it is clearly a Matter badge, and it is one block in SharePage.vue: the day certification is earned, the certified mark replaces it there and nowhere else. An e2e test asserts the page never says “certified”.

NAMING THE STANDARD IN TEXT IS FINE AND IS NOT WHAT THIS IS ABOUT. “Works with Matter”, “becomes a Matter device”, and the three app names are ordinary nominative use, and the page leans on all of them.
